title: I'm 42. My biggest regret? Not taking enough risks in my 20s (exited startups to Apple & Discord)
guest: John Redgrave, founder and GP of DTX Ventures, serial entrepreneur who sold machine-learning companies to Apple and Discord, early Palantir employee
summary: A rapid-fire conversation with cybersecurity entrepreneur and investor John Redgrave, followed by the sisters' takeaways. Redgrave's advice to his younger self is to take risks sooner and become an incredible storyteller; he reframes rejection as micro failures and 'no as a gift', and gives a three-part public speaking method (stay on message, stay calm, do reps) including using ChatGPT as a mock interviewer. The hosts add a physical warm-up trick for nerves, a call to study diverse storytellers, and a challenge to fail small this week.

ideas.idea: The number one advice to a 29-year-old is to take risks sooner in life, professionally and personally, because the only thing stopping you from creating what you want is usually yourself.
ideas.detail: Type A people in particular take fewer risks than they could because of fear of failure. Redgrave, now 42, calls this his biggest regret.

ideas.idea: Become an incredible storyteller, because storytelling drives recruiting, fundraising, selling and nearly all institutional change.
ideas.detail: Build the skill by mimicking great storytellers from music, the arts and corporate America (Steve Jobs). Narrow exposure means telling stories through one lens; you must tailor the story to the people you are trying to move.

ideas.idea: Rules are generally put in place to stifle innovation, so figure out which rules are meant to be broken and break them mindfully.
ideas.detail: Redgrave was always a rule breaker as a kid and believes that is what makes him a good entrepreneur, even as he tries to teach his own kids otherwise. The hosts dub it 'mindful rule breaking'.

ideas.idea: Entrepreneurship starts with identifying a market need and realizing no one but you will address it, so the outcome rides entirely on your own effort.
ideas.detail: His first job was building a web solutions business in the 1990s making websites for small and medium businesses. His work ethic came from family who worked hard for everything with nothing given, and he tells his kids daily that hard work brings good things.

ideas.idea: Life is a series of micro failures; hearing 'no' more often is a signal to change how you approach problems and people, and a no today may be a gift that opens a better yes later.
ideas.detail: Applies beyond career to raising kids, school and love life. Successful people 'incept' failures in their mind as things they turned around and focus on the learning rather than the mistake, running through brick walls by going through, around or over obstacles.

ideas.idea: Humans learn more from failure than success, so if you never put yourself in a position where you might fail you are fundamentally capping your potential.
ideas.detail: Both Redgrave and Cherie took classes from Stanford GSB professor Joel Peterson, who told students their biggest problem was that they had not failed enough; Redgrave only truly experienced failure once he started building companies.

ideas.idea: Hot take: the US is at least six months ahead of China on AI, partly because America is bad at regulating technology, which accrues an advantage.
ideas.detail: Most Americans are scared of AI, China, or both, and do not realize weak regulation plus a talent edge keeps the US ahead.

ideas.idea: Public speaking rule one: it is your message, and any question can be bridged back to your core talking points however long it takes.
ideas.detail: Learned through media training, a Frontline special and being grilled by aggressive interviewers and government officials worldwide. The hosts compare it to debate candidates who pivot from a question about the LA fires to the state budget.

ideas.idea: Public speaking rule two: stay calm and breathe, because visible nerves (shaky voice or hands) erode your message by signaling you lack confidence.
ideas.detail: Even if you are sweating through your jacket, remain cool under pressure; confidence is the key.

ideas.idea: Public speaking rule three: do tons of reps, and use ChatGPT as a mock interviewer to generate 20-30 likely questions, grill you, and grade your answers.
ideas.detail: Redgrave prepped with former investigative reporters and then talked to ChatGPT on car rides; ask it to rate a response one to ten, or build a custom GPT trained on a media prep deck to tune each answer. The hosts praised this as the most actionable advice of the season.

ideas.idea: Do a two-to-three-minute physical warm-up like ten jumping jacks before a presentation so your racing heart rate matches what your body is doing.
ideas.detail: Cherie's former boss Eric taught her that the mismatch between adrenaline and standing still is what feels like nerves; a brief 'body pump' makes the state feel congruous without leaving you out of breath.

ideas.idea: Model your storytelling on a diverse set of speakers, not just tech founders like Steve Jobs, so your style is not one narrow lens.
ideas.detail: The hosts list Martin Luther King Jr., Winston Churchill, Walter Cronkite, Oprah (who can say what a million others have said, e.g. how GLP-1s quiet food noise, and be the face of trust), Michelle Obama, Jon Stewart, and actors who tell stories on behalf of others.

ideas.idea: Great leaders answer unprepped questions compellingly because they have already done deep reflection on their own story.
ideas.detail: No guest in the series was given questions ahead of time or had PR prep; the hosts note the podcast itself is their reps for speaking extemporaneously, since a narrative often sounds smoother in your head than out loud.

ideas.idea: High achievers who have never failed face a harder fall: the higher you climb before your first failure, the more devastating and harder to recover from it is, so seek micro failures early to build 'bouncy bones'.
ideas.detail: Jean's analogy of little kids bouncing when they fall learning to ski versus an older person with brittle bones; the hosts link it to 'failure training' from David Shim's episode. Actionable takeaway: ask what small thing outside your comfort zone you can try and possibly fail at this week.

ideas.idea: Conferences are about the people: get outside the core business context, break bread, and use the shared host as an icebreaker.
ideas.detail: Redgrave attends Imran's conference for the friends at the cutting edge of their industries and was especially interested in conversations on AI and national security, because investing in the future is what matters.
